findings.explanation: `res.render(view, options, callback)` treats a function-valued second argument as the callback and otherwise uses `options || {}`, so null/undefined become an empty object. It obtains the application from `res.req.app`, overwrites `_locals` on the options object with this response's locals, and delegates to `app.render`. During normal request setup, `res.locals` is initialized to an empty null-prototype object if absent. Without a truthy callback, the generated callback forwards errors to `req.next(err)` and sends successful output with `res.send`. Supplying a callback disables both automatic actions; the caller owns error handling and sending. There is no callback type guard beyond this truthiness/function normalization.

Spread order establishes precedence: explicit render options override response locals (`opts._locals`), which override `app.locals`. Direct `app.render` also maps null/undefined options to `{}` and accepts the callback as its second argument. A merged `cache` value of null or undefined falls back to the `view cache` setting; explicit false or another non-null falsy value disables caching, while true/truthy enables it. A fresh top-level app enables `view cache` automatically only when `NODE_ENV` is `production` (the environment otherwise defaults to `development`). The cache contains View objects keyed by the requested name. A hit skips construction and lookup. On a miss, a successfully located View is inserted before `tryRender`, so a subsequent render error does not remove it; a View with no path is reported and never inserted. This differs from `app.engines`: registered or auto-loaded engine functions remain in that registry independently of View caching, while any engine-internal compiled-template caching is not established by this code.

The built-in View takes `path.extname(name)` first. An explicit filename extension selects that extension's engine and does not use the default engine. Without an extension, a configured default engine is normalized to a leading dot and appended to the lookup filename; without either, construction throws. A fresh app configures this built-in View and a default views root of `resolve('views')`, but no default view engine. A truthy existing `opts.engines[ext]` is reused. Otherwise Express requires the extension name without its dot, reads `__express`, requires it to be a function, and stores it for later Views—even when View caching is disabled. `app.engine` is the supported registration path: it normalizes the leading dot and rejects non-functions, although direct mutation of `app.engines` can bypass that guard. Module-resolution/evaluation errors and invalid `__express` errors propagate synchronously from construction. The View class itself is configurable through the `view` setting, so these selection rules apply only while the default implementation is in use.

`lookup` converts the configured root to an array and examines roots in array order, stopping at the first match. Within each root it resolves the requested name and calls this resolver, so root 1's direct file and index fallback are both attempted before root 2. The direct candidate is checked first; then `foo.ext` falls back to `foo/index.ext`. Both candidates must have a successful stat whose result reports `isFile()`, so directories and other non-regular results are rejected. `tryStat` uses synchronous `fs.statSync` but catches every stat exception and returns undefined, treating missing, inaccessible, and other stat failures alike. If both candidates fail, resolution returns undefined and lookup continues; exhaustion leaves `view.path` undefined. Only stat failures are swallowed—invalid path operations outside `tryStat` can still throw.

The catch boundary begins only when `tryRender` invokes `view.render`. Therefore synchronous throws from that call—including a synchronous engine throw under the built-in View—are converted to `callback(err)`. It cannot catch later asynchronous throws, and an exception thrown by `callback(err)` itself escapes. Earlier, `app.render` constructs the configured View outside this boundary. Constructor failures—including no extension/default engine, module-loading failures, invalid `__express`, or a custom constructor throw—therefore propagate synchronously rather than being delivered to the render callback. An ordinary unsuccessful built-in lookup is different: construction completes with no `view.path`, after which `app.render` creates a missing-view Error, attaches `err.view`, and immediately returns `done(err)` before caching or rendering. When errors are delivered through `done`, default `res.render` calls `req.next(err)`; an explicit response callback receives them itself. Constructor throws bypass that default callback at this layer.

The built-in View delegates to its configured engine with `(path, options, onRender)`. If the engine invokes `onRender` before the engine function returns, View copies every argument plus the invocation context and delivers them on `process.nextTick`. Once the engine has returned, later callbacks are forwarded immediately at the engine's own asynchronous timing with the same arguments and context. This wrapper does not enforce at-most-once delivery: every synchronous invocation schedules a tick and every later invocation is forwarded. A concrete duplicate path is an engine that calls back synchronously and then throws—the scheduled result remains while `tryRender` also reports the throw. An engine that calls back repeatedly, or once before throwing and again later, likewise causes repeated delivery; an engine that never calls back produces none. These timing rules are proven only for the built-in View wrapper. A custom View can bypass them, and the configured engine's actual callback timing and multiplicity are unconstrained by this source.
